utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Paul Rogers for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Priya Gopalan and our case manager today, Ms. Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Rogers. For Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Ben Emmerson for Mr. Haradinaj, together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, and Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Emmerson. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Gregor Guy-Smith, with Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and Mr. Zyberi continues to be with us on behalf of Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. For Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Richard Harvey with Mr. Paul Troop and Ms. Sophie Rigney for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you render your decision, may I just thank you for the time that you gave us this morning to enable me to just resolve one or two matters with Mr. Karnavas. It related to some medical notes that he provided to me from his client which I've managed to now distribute to my learned friends and I wanted to just put that on record, if there was anything they wanted to raise relating to that before Your Honours are about to render your decision, if you are going to render your decision, I wanted to just give them that opportunity, if they wanted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to allow the Chamber to run the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will render the decision because we know nothing about medical records right now. So, let us do what we anticipate rather than what we don't anticipate. I did say good morning to everybody. Yes. Yesterday we had an oral application and the Chamber is about to give its decision. The Chamber is seized of an oral application made by the Prosecution in court on the 23rd of August, 2011, to admit into evidence in the present proceedings the transcript of Shefqet Kabashi's evidence in the Limaj case as evidence for the truth of its contents. It is submitted that the witness has stated under oath on a number of occasions that the content of this evidence is true. Reference is made in particular to transcript pages 385 and 401 of the hearing of the 22nd of August, 2011, and transcript page 426 of the hearing of 23rd August. It is submitted that the proposed evidence is relevant and probative and can be received under 89(C) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The application is opposed by the accused. Counsel for Haradinaj submits that it is not open to the Prosecution to rely on Rule 89 if the specific requirements of Rule 92 bis and Rule 92 ter are not capable -- capable of being satisfied. With respect to Rule 92 ter it is submitted that the witness is not available for cross-examination in that while present in the courtroom he has indicated that he's unable or unwilling to answer questions on the substance, whether from the Prosecution or from the Defence, and that the witness has not stated that the transcript accurately reflects what he would have said if examined before the Tribunal. The position advanced is that if the Prosecution cannot satisfy the requirements of Rule 92 ter, it is not entitled to rely on any general provision in Rule 89. Reference is made to Appeals Chamber jurisprudence, in particular to the Galic decision of June 2002 and to the Milosevic decision of 30th September 2003 in support of the submission that unless the requirements of Rule 92 bis were satisfied, there was no scope for invoking Rule 89(C). Counsel for Balaj and Brahimaj joined the Haradinaj Defence in these decisions. In his reply, counsel for the Prosecution submits, inter alia, that it was never the Prosecution's intent to call this witness under Rule 92 ter because it was felt appropriate for this witness to give evidence orally. He submits that the witness gave some limited evidence orally and that Rule 92 ter is usually applied before a witness has come and started to give viva voce evidence. The present application concerns the admissibility of a transcript of the prior testimony of a witness before this Tribunal for the truth of its contents. The procedure for submission of written statements and transcripts in lieu of oral testimony is provided for by Rule 92 bis of the Rules. Rule 92 bis gives discretion to the Trial Chamber to admit written statements or transcripts of prior evidence of witnesses, provided that certain conditions listed in the rule and elaborated on in the jurisprudence are met. The Appeals Chamber has commented on the application of Rule 92 bis and Rule 89(C) to witness statement and transcripts of prior evidence of a witness. It has held that a party cannot be permitted to tender a written statement or transcript under Rule 89(C) in order to avoid the stringency of Rule 92 bis. That is Galic decision, paragraph 31. As explained by the Appeals Chamber in Galic decision, paragraphs 28 and 30, and Milosevic decision of 30th September 2003, paragraph 18, subparagraph 3, Rule 92 bis as a whole is concerned with one very special type of hearsay evidence which would previously have been admissible under Rule 89(C), namely, written statements given by prospective witnesses for the purposes of legal proceedings. Because of the need to ensure reliability of the admitted evidence in such circumstances, the Appeals Chamber has held that Rule 92 bis is the lex specialis which takes the admissibility of such written statements of prospective witnesses and transcripts of evidence out of the scope of the lex generalis of Rule 89(C). Although the general provisions implicit in Rule 89(C) remain applicable to Rule 92 bis. That's the Galic decision paragraph 31 and Milosevic decision of 30th September, 2003, paragraph 18(3). The Appeals Chamber has made clear in its jurisprudence, however, that Rule 92 bis does not exclude the admission of written statements or transcripts in all circumstances. It has held that where Rule 92 bis is applicable, the requirements of Rule 92 bis must be met but the prohibition of Rule 92 bis does not extend to material not governed by Rule 92 bis. That's Milosevic decision of 30th September 2003, paragraphs 9 and 10. It has held that a written statement given by prospective witnesses to OTP investigators or others for the purpose of legal proceedings may be admitted into evidence "notwithstanding its noncompliance with Rule 92 bis - (i) where there has been no objection taken to it or (ii) where it has otherwise become admissible, for example, the written statement is asserted to contain a prior statement inconsistent with the witness's evidence." Milosevic decision of 30th September 2003, paragraph 18 and paragraph 14. Other examples of material not governed by Rule 92 bis given by the Appeals Chamber include hearsay material which has not -- was not prepared for the purposes of legal proceedings, for example, a report prepared not for the purpose of legal proceedings or situations where the witness is present in court and can orally attest to the accuracy of the written statement. Paragraph 16 of the Milosevic decision of 30th November -- September 2003. In the Chamber's view, Rule 92 bis is not applicable in the present situation. The witness was called to give evidence viva voce. He commenced giving evidence and in fact did give some evidence orally. The witness then started that -- stated, I beg your pardon -- the witness then stated that he cannot answer the Prosecution's questions. It became clear in the course of his examination-in-chief that his disposition before this Chamber is inconsistent with his disposition in the Limaj case, to the extent that in the latter case he was able to answer the question put to him by the Prosecution, questions to the same events as the questions put to him in the present case, and was able to provide an account of the relevant events. In the view of the Chamber, the present situation is one of the situations specifically envisaged by the Appeals Chamber where the written evidence may be admitted. The Chamber is satisfied that in the present circumstances Rule 92 bis is not the lex specialis which excludes the applicability of Rule 89(C). It should be noted that in many jurisdictions a special procedure is to be followed in cases where a party calling a witness wishes to cross-examine the witness or tender his prior witness statement for the truth of its contents. The Appeals Chamber has confirmed that in this Tribunal it is for the Trial Chamber hearing the case to decide whether to allow a party to put a prior statement to its own witness and cross-examine that witness. This decision may or may not be done on the basis of a prior determination of hostility. Popovic decision of 1st February 2008 at paragraph 28. It was put to the Chamber that if the requirements of Rule 92 ter are not satisfied, the Prosecution is not entitled to rely on any general provision in Rule 89. In the Chamber's view, Rule 92 ter does not apply in the present circumstances. As held in the jurisprudence, the main objective of Rule 92 ter is to ensure an effective and expeditious trial while respecting the rights of the accused. And we can see for that Prlic decision of the 21st of July, 2007, and the Delic decision of the 27th of September, 2007, and those are Trial Chamber's decisions. Rule 92 ter is concerned with the mode in which a witness gives evidence, whether entirely viva voce or whether his evidence in chief may be admitted in written form if a witness is present in court, available for cross-examination, and attests that the statement or transcript in question adequately reflect what the witness would say if examined. In other words, Rule 92 ter is not intended to replace the oral evidence of a witness. It was precisely for this reason why the Appeals Chamber excluded situations where a witness is present in court, available for cross-examination, and any questioning by the Judges and, and attests that the statement accurately reflects his or her declaration and what he or she would say if examined from the scope of application of Rule 92 bis. For that you can see paragraph 16 of the Milosevic decision of the 30th of September, 2003. The Chamber would note that the Milosevic decision of the same date I've just mentioned was issued before the adoption of Rule 92 ter in 2006, and Rule 92 ter to a large extent is based on that decision. The Chamber turns now to consider whether the proposed transcript is admissible under Rule 89(C). Under Rule 89(C), the Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The Chamber is satisfied that the proposed transcript is both relevant and of probative value. The proposed transcript relates to the witness's knowledge about two men, Pal Krasniqi and Skender Kuci, who are victims of the acts alleged in the indictment and to other matters relevant to the present indictment. The witness gave evidence under oath before another Chamber at this Tribunal. He was examined before the Trial Chamber in Limaj by the Prosecution and cross-examined by the three Defence teams in that case. The witness confirmed before that Chamber that his evidence in the Limaj case was truthful and so he did before this Chamber. Rule 89(C) grants the Chamber broad discretion. The Appeals Chamber has held that this discretion must be exercised "in harmony with the Statute and the other Rules to the greatest extent possible." Kordic decision of 21st July 2000, paragraph 20; Galic decision, paragraph 27, the Galic decision that we have referred to earlier. The Chamber therefore will consider whether the admission of the proposed transcript in the present circumstances is in the interests of justice and whether it may cause the accused prejudice. No parts of Rule 92, indeed no other rule, anticipates such a situation as now arises where a witness called to give viva voce evidence and having made the solemn declaration declares himself unwilling or unable to answer pertinent questions put by the party calling him. The evidence sought to be tendered by the Prosecution is, short of viva voce testimony, the best evidence obtainable. It is testimony of the witness in proceedings before this Tribunal where there was full opportunity for cross-examination by a counsel of the parties on the opposing side and where there is no indication from the record that the witness had any reservations or difficulties in being able to testify. With respect to whether the admission of the document will cause prejudice to the rights of the accused, the Chamber notes in this respect that its decision to admit the transcript pursuant to Rule 89(C) will not preclude the Defence from cross-examining the witness. Considering the conduct of the witness yesterday and the day before, the Chamber is mindful that the witness may refuse to answer questions from the Defence. Should this be the case, the Chamber will be open to admit, pursuant to Rule 89(C), any documents or other items that any of the Defence teams had intended to put to the witness in cross-examination but were unable to do so because of his behaviour. The Chamber also will take into account the extent to which the witness was examined and cross-examined when determining the weight to be given to the proposed transcript. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber decides to admit the transcript of Shefqet Kabashi's testimony in the Limaj case. The Chamber will request Madam Registrar to assign an exhibit number to the admitted document. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we give them separate exhibit numbers, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, before Your Honour formally admits them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would like, if I may, to ask you to rise for approximately 15 minutes so that the Defence teams can consult as to whether to make representations to you as to the continuance of the trial at this stage. In other words, we would like to consider amongst ourselves whether to invite the Trial Chamber to pause with a view to considering whether there ought to be an interlocutory appeal. That is a matter which obviously we would need to consult amongst one another about and obviously we haven't had Your Honours' decisional reasons and haven't had an opportunity to do that. There is another alternative possibility which is under consideration which is that we may apply under Rule 89(D) for the exclusion of the transcript that Your Honours currently propose to admit once the evidence of this witness is concluded if it is to continue. It may well be that matters occur hereafter which will form the basis of an application under 89(D) to exclude. Now, it may be in those circumstances once it has been marked and given its exhibit number Your Honours will think it appropriate to have given the ruling but formally to admit the transcript, if you are to do so, at the very end of the witness's evidence. I'm sorry if that sounds rather confusing. What I'm immediately inviting Your Honours to do is to rise for a short time so that the Defence teams can take instructions from their clients and to consult amongst themselves as to what is the appropriate next step and to secure the position by not formally admitting the transcript at this moment in time because there may be further submissions to be made to this Trial Chamber in the light of the way that the witness's evidence hereafter progresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could you enlighten me as to -- you made reference to 89(D), and unless I'm missing something the ruling that the Chamber has just given would, I would have thought, have dealt with that. Could you tell me what I'm missing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, clearly no ruling on admissibility can be immutable. Events may occur in the course of the remainder of this witness's evidence which enable the Defence, entitle the Defence, to make an application that an item of evidence be excluded. Now, it is possible, I imagine, certainly in most jurisdictions for the Trial Chamber to exclude evidence after it has been admitted, indeed in the first trial that happened in relation to one witness who refused to be cross-examined. The Trial Chamber took the view that his evidence should be struck from the record and his evidence in chief was excluded. I'm simply at this stage suggesting that it -- giving that timing doesn't matter, giving that it can be formally admitted if the Trial Chamber takes the view that that's the right course after the witness's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think I now follow you, but that wouldn't prevent what the Chamber has now ordered for the registrar to assign exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I'm simply saying there are two ways in which a subsequent application might procedurally be considered and ruled upon were the Trial Chamber of the view in due course that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I now get you, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I don't get, Mr. Emmerson, is the reason for adjournment for 15 minutes. If the parties would like to take instructions from their clients and appeal the decision, they can do so even at the next break, but I don't seem to see why we should break right now. It's not a matter of life and death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, Your Honour, it's certainly not a matter of life and death, but there's certainly no reason to rush into the next portion of these proceedings. And I think it would be prudent and responsible for Defence counsel to meet for a moment and for Defence counsel to meet with their clients, considering that we just received this decision and we had no way of knowing which way the Chamber would rule on this issue. 15 minutes of time at this moment might save us hours of time later, and clearly I think we all do appreciate that this particular ruling is rather important with regard to the progress of these particular proceedings. And I would -- I would -- if 15 minutes is too much, then I would ask for 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will give you 14 and a half. Except, I just want to make this comment, I would like to know in which jurisdiction counsel or parties ever do know in advance what a decision of the Chamber is going to be? We will rise for 15 minutes. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 9.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Thank you for the time you allowed us. We have no representations or applications to make at this moment in time and therefore the evidence of the witness can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Registrar, can you please assign a number to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the redacted transcript, 65 ter 03047 will be Exhibit P119; and the full transcript 65 ter 03047.1 will be Exhibit P120 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May the witness be re-called, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kabashi. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the light of Your Honours' ruling and the admission of the Limaj transcript into evidence in this case, Your Honours, in light of the past conduct of the witness and the attempts to extract testimony from him over the last few days, the Prosecution does not intend to ask any further questions and to allow him now to be cross-examined by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, yesterday you told Mr. Rogers that you felt unable to answer any further questions about the events in 1998 in Jabllanice, not that you didn't want to but that you felt that you were unable to answer questions. Does that remain your position?

Does that remain your position as I'm speaking to you right now?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]

utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS

utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Kabashi, thank you very much for taking the time to come and testify in the Tribunal in this case. We have now come to the end of your testimony. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before Mr. Rogers continues, as I indicated to Your Honours earlier on, an application is now being made under Rule 89(D) for the exclusion of the transcript and I want, if I may, to outline the reasons for that. There is then an alternative application made under Rule 89(D) to exclude all portions of the transcript other than the one that Mr. Rogers relied upon and that Your Honours referred to concerning Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi. Can I indicate what the basis for this application is? First of all, we are dealing now with a situation where a witness has refused to be cross-examined. The Defence have been deprived of the opportunity of putting questions to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Deprived?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly, by the witness. When a witness refuses to answer questions or doesn't return for cross-examination, the Defence are deprived of an essential fair trial right. The position, if I can take the application on its broadest footing first of all is that whilst it's right that this witness gave evidence in the Limaj trial - I don't know whether Your Honours have had an opportunity yet to read the transcript - the vast bulk of it has nothing whatsoever to do with Jabllanice and no questions were put by any of the Defence counsel in the original Limaj trial concerning Jabllanice. Jabllanice formed no part of the indictment against any of the Limaj defendants and all questions that were put to this witness in cross-examination by counsel, none of whom was representing any one of these accused, concerned any of the matters that are relevant to this trial. So the suggestion that -- upon which Your Honours appear to have placed some weight, that the transcript had the additional authenticity or validity that it had been subjected to cross-examination, has no purchase whatever on those portions of the transcript which are relevant to these proceedings. That's the first point. The second point is that to deny or for the Defence to be denied of the opportunity to cross-examine is a matter which strikes at the root of fair trial rights. We are dealing here with a witness who on the Prosecution's case - and indeed in the view of the Appeals Chamber - is central. A witness of considerable importance. And it must be the case that the fair trial rights of the accused, and in particular the right to confront and effectively to cross-examine the witness, acquire even greater importance when the witness is central in these proceedings; and greater still where his testimony is uncorroborated. I'll come to the question of corroboration in a moment. The third principal point I'd like to make, if I may, is that in the ruling Your Honours gave in principle, Your Honours indicated that there had been answers given by the witness, indicating that the testimony he had given in Limaj was true. Your Honours did not refer - and I simply remind you of it by reference - to all of the passages from yesterday's testimony when the witness said the reverse. That's page 424, lines 1 to 3; page 425, lines 10 to 15; page 425, lines 21 to 25, when the witness said in terms that he could not stand over his testimony in Limaj and did not know now whether it was accurate and reliable; and page 426, lines 5 to 9, when asked about whether it was reliable, he says, "That is where the problem lies. I can't recall that time." Now, that being the case, the balance that Your Honours have struck needs to be, we submit, attenuated. In the previous trial and for these purposes I refer to this only because it is a ruling of law of a Trial Chamber, not because it is a ruling of law in an earlier trial in these proceedings, but a witness who was given the pseudonym 55 was called and gave evidence in chief, was asked one or two foundation questions in cross-examination, and his testimony was then adjourned. Thereafter, he refused to return to be cross-examined. The Trial Chamber conducted an examination of his medical fitness and concluded in the event, particularly having regard to issues concerning his mental health, that they would not order that he attend to be cross-examined and invited submissions of the parties as to whether or not a fair trial, as envisaged in Rule 89(D), required the exclusion of the testimony of the witness, where the Defence were unable to complete an effective cross-examination, notwithstanding, as here, that the witness had in fact attended to give evidence. If I can just give Your Honours the reference, it's the reasons for the Trial Chamber's decision to exclude the evidence of Witness 55 under Rule 89(D) and deny his testimony pursuant to 92 quater of the 14th of December, 2007. So the question for the Trial Chamber was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But, as I say, I rely on it not because it is this case but because it is a ruling in analogous factual circumstances. And the application of the Prosecution was that the evidence in chief should remain on the record, notwithstanding the inability of the Defence to cross-examine because the witness refused to return and alternatively, that the transcript should be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 quater on the grounds of the witness's mental health. Both applications were refused, and if I can just read to Your Honours from paragraph 10 of the decision. "In considering whether to exclude the testimony of Witness 55, the Chamber agreed with the Prosecution that Witness 55's testimony is relevant to Haradinaj's alleged direct participation in crimes in the joint criminal enterprise charged in the indictment, the alleged conflict between the KLA and FARK, the command structure within the KLA during the indictment period, and the alleged KLA use of the Lake Radoniq canal as a dump site for bodies. The testimony therefore relates to central issues in the case, including the acts and conduct of one of the accused and is of a pivotal nature." Pausing there, this witness's testimony does not in fact concern the acts and conduct of the accused of Mr. Haradinaj. The evidence that you've just admitted makes no mention of any acts and conduct of Mr. Haradinaj, but it does in relation to other accused. So it does concern the acts and conduct of the accused. "The testimony therefore relates to central issues in the case including the acts and conduct of one of the accused of a pivotal nature. The Chamber considers under these circumstances the lack of cross-examination would mean that the probative value of the testimony is substantially outweighed by the accused's right to a fair trial. Unless the Chamber is satisfied as to the reliability of the witnesses's testimony, and with there also being strong corroboration from other witnesses as to the central allegation." And on the basis of the application of that test, the witness's testimony was struck from the record and the Prosecution's application under Rule 92 quater refused. Now, in these proceedings, particularly if Your Honours were to refresh your memories from the passages of the transcript I read -- I identified just a moment ago, which didn't find mention in the ruling but which go substantially against the proposition that this witness stands over the detail of his testimony. Indeed, he said in terms to Your Honours that he could not do that. That was his evidence yesterday. There's simply no escaping from it. One cannot cherry-pick from one part of the transcript and ignore the rest. On a fair reading of the witness's testimony yesterday he was not prepared to say which parts, if any, of the Limaj transcript were accurate and which were not. So we're left with a situation where he's not available for cross-examination. There's no question, with the greatest of respect, of documents being put to the witness as a substitute for cross-examination. It can't possibly substitute for the right to confront and cross-examine just as the documents that could have been put to the Witness 55 couldn't substitute for it for the opportunity to confront and for the Trial Chamber to evaluate. The balance has now tipped decisively, we would say, in favour of a fair trial. Rule 89(D) specifically requires the Chamber to balance the probative value of the evidence against the fair trial rights of the accused. Well, Your Honours haven't read the evidence, so it would be difficult for you to yet have formed a view as to its probative value. So that is an exercise Your Honours cannot yet have performed. So we are going to invite you to reconsider in the light of those matters the substance of the transcript. Now, the position is this: Anything that does not have to do with Jabllanice in the transcript is irrelevant. Its probative value is nil in these proceedings. Anything which has to do with Jabllanice but which is uncorroborated is also, given the witness's position, of very limited probative weight. The only aspect of his testimony in the Limaj case in which the Prosecution sought to rely and on which Your Honours relied in the ruling that you just gave was the fact that the witness had answered questions in Limaj about Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi but had given different answers in these proceedings or none at all. The allegations concerning Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi are supported by other evidence. To that extent, that part of this witness's testimony in Limaj is capable of some corroboration. But anything extending outside of that is of minimal or no probative value when weighed against, first, a fair reading of yesterday's transcript and what the witness said about his ability to stand over it; and secondly, the absolute denial of any opportunity to cross-examine. And so we would respectfully invite Your Honours to perform the exercise which, as a matter of logic, you cannot yet have performed, namely, to evaluate what really is the probative value of this material. And we would submit that weighed against the unfairness to the accused, it is as a whole outweighed and should be excluded under 89(D); or in the alternative, that the only passages that should be included, and I can give you the references for them in just a moment, they would be 4255 to 4260 private session in the transcript are those which relate to those two witnesses, the basis of the application, and the basis of Your Honours' ruling, and that the remainder of the transcript in the alternative should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Emmerson, before you sit down. In -- you've referred to Witness 55 in this -- in this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in the previous proceedings. Did you have opportunity to look at the Martic trial record with respect to the testimony of Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, but I can do certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I invite you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm -- may I invite Your Honours to consider the decision in these proceedings in relation to Witness 5 -- 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But obviously, each case in the end is going to turn on its facts. What I take from that decision is that if the more important and relevant the evidence, the greater the injustice of denying cross-examination, first of all. Secondly, that in the absence of corroboration of the testimony, denial of cross-examination will be decisive for the fairness of the proceedings. Those are principles, not applications to the facts. Applying them to these facts you only have one passage of this evidence, which is relevant, directly probative, and corroborated, and it's the passage that Mr. Rogers relied on and the passage that Your Honours relied on without having read the transcript first. There is a vast amount of material that cannot begin to cross the threshold of probative weight which would enable it to be sufficient to outweigh the unfairness to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would join in the remarks that have just been made by Mr. Emmerson. I would also highlight that cross-examination is a minimum guaranteed right under our Statute, Article 21(iv)(e) under the ICCPR, the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights, Article 14(iii)(e); and the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 6(iii)(d). The recognition of the importance of cross-examination in order to obtain in the crucible of the trial the truth requires not only the ability for the party to be able to engage in cross-examination and which we have not had, but also it's important because it allows the fact-finder, Your Honours, in this particular situation to have a full and complete record and understanding of that testimony, which you do not have. With regard to Babic, I think there are two things and I'm not -- you said Martic and I went straight to Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did say Babic, I said the testimony of Babic in the Martic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A case which I believe you are intimately familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not so quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I recall -- and if memory fails me then I do apologise, but just briefly and if it needs further discussion I'm happy to have that at a later point in time. If I recall, there was the ability in that case for some specific, focused examination by counsel of the witness concerning his testimony which was truncated as a result of his death. The application for the inclusion of Mr. Babic's testimony, as I recall, was made under 92 quater, if I'm not mistaken, and there were some considerations by virtue of the fact it was made under that particular rule, that particular lex specialis rule, that also impacted upon the Chamber's decision. But most importantly what has -- what existed there and what does not exist here and what the Limaj transcript makes abundantly clear, which I think is in contrast to what was said in today's decision, I believe was on page 9 - I could be mistaken - is that counsel had some ability to engage in a focused cross-examination of the issues that were germane to that case. And as Mr. Rogers indicated, as I mentioned the other day, Limaj was focused on entirely different issues. It was not focused on the issue of Jabllanice. Counsel in that case was neither instructed nor attentive to the issues of Jabllanice because they did not factor into the Limaj case. To foreclose -- to be in a situation where cross-examination is effectively foreclosed and to entertain this particular evidence, in my submission, is fundamentally unfair. It strikes at the foundation stones of a system of justice. And by "foundation stones" I mean that in an institutional sense to proceed down this line and to not the exclude this evidence is exceedingly dangerous, not only in this case but also with regard to the evolution of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you sit down, Mr. Guy-Smith, could you make yourself quite clear, like Mr. Emmerson did, do you want the exclusion of the entire evidence or do you want the exclusion of a portion of the evidence that is -- that you would say is irrelevant to these proceedings but for the evidence relating to Pal Krasniqi and Kuci?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join in the remarks that were made by Mr. Emmerson specifically in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also join in all of the remarks made by both Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith. I would add this just, if I may, to remind the Trial Chamber, that Mr. Brahimaj does not stand before you in relation to either Mr. Skender Kuci or Pal Krasniqi. I just make that point. I know it's much in your minds. That the transcripts that are now P119 and P120 are of evidence taken before any of these three accused appeared before this Court, and therefore none of them had representation at that time. No representations could have been made on their behalf in relation to evidence that might affect them. I am not even sure if they had been arrested at that time. I think they were arrested -- they were certainly arrested in that month, but I don't believe they had actually been arrested at the date of those transcripts. But I don't wish to add anything to what has been said. I wish to adopt everything that Mr. Emmerson said in relation to the admissibility and relevance of those transcripts under 89(D). I would just because there is an error in the transcript of today's argument before Your Honours, Mr. Emmerson at page 20, line 13 is correctly quoted as saying: Pausing there, this witness's testimony, that's Mr. Kabashi in Limaj, does not in fact concern the acts and conduct of the accused Mr. Haradinaj, that's correct, but the next sentence is not. The next sentence reads: It does not make any mention of the acts and conduct of the accused. As you will recall, I believe Mr. Emmerson clearly stated the testimony does make mention of the acts and conduct of the other two accused. So it does have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give that reference again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Page 20 today, lines 13 to 15. I hope that makes matters clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might, I want to correct myself because I said 92 quater with regard to the Babic situation and I was incorrect. And knowing the way things are going right now, I want to make sure I have not made a misrepresentation to the Chamber. As I understand it it was made under 89(C) and (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand that we do make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would point out with regard to that decision at paragraph 70 the following was stated: "The Trial Chamber knows that Milan Babic testified for approximately 25 hours in court under oath in the presence of the accused. His cross-examination lasted approximately 10.5 hours. The Trial Chamber finds that the completed cross-examination up to the date of death was sufficient for the Trial Chamber to fairly judge the credibility and reliability of Milan Babic as a witness." Those factors are non-existent in this case at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, can I just clarify Mr. Harvey's point in case there should be any misunderstanding about it what I thought I had said and certainly what the position is, and I think we can all agree on this, is that the testimony that you have just considered and ruled upon the admission of and about which this present application is made, makes no allegations concerning the acts and conduct of Mr. Haradinaj but does make allegations concerning the acts and conduct of Mr. Balaj and Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that's not -- that's not specifically correct, and to the extent that -- to the extent that -- I would not disagree with Mr. Emmerson as it relates to Mr. Haradinaj. I would disagree with Mr. Emmerson as it relates to Mr. Balaj because once you read it you will see that it is made in a generalised sense without there being any specificity as to any particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should correct myself to this extent. There is no dispute that the testimony makes specific reference to the acts and conduct of Mr. Brahimaj, and to that extent it concerns the acts and conduct of the accused. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out if counsel would not want to have a short adjournment just to make sure that they're at one on what representations have to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think we are at one. There is limited reference to Mr. Brahimaj. Of course he was not represented in those proceedings. There was no cross-examination in relation to him whatsoever. There was no cross-examination in relation to Jabllanice. There is a limited reference to his presence and by implication acts and conduct. I think that's as far as it can go and I think we're all agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Rogers, do you have anything to contribute to the debate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, I hope so, Your Honour. Whether you find it a useful contribution of course will be a matter for Your Honours in due course. Yes, I do. The application is made under Rule 89(D), and it's on the basis that the Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to have a fair trial. My learned friends mount their challenge on two bases. First, they say that there is no probative value to this material, and secondly, they say it's unfair to them to admit it, it having already been admitted, because they have no right to cross-examine. They do have a right to cross-examine. The fundamental basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not misrepresent, Mr. Rogers. They don't say they don't have the right to cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- they said they were precluded, foreclosed, if I might use Mr. Guy-Smith's phrase, term, from

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, but effectively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the right they have, and they did exercise it. They asked him one question each.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, and they say because they -- the witness answered in a single way that that meant effectively they had no effective right to cross-examine. It's a denial by the witness of the right to cross-examine. Your Honours, that's simply not the case. My learned friends have an opportunity, if they wished, to explore with the witness further the reasons for his wish not to continue to testify, the basis for that, and to test them to such extent as they considered appropriate on any of the matters contained in the Limaj trial and to elicit from him such answers as he was or was not prepared to give. My learned friends have chosen instead - and it's entirely a matter for them how they wish to conduct their cross-examinations - but they've chosen to answer a single question -- ask a single question: "You told Mr. Rogers that you felt unable to answer any further questions about the events in 1998, not that you didn't want to, but you felt that you were unable to answer questions. Does that remain your position? "A. Yes." That's Mr. Emmerson at page 14, lines 23, to page 15, line 2. And they meekly, respectfully, accept that answer. They don't take any attempt to go further with it. I accept that he -- the witness simply says, "I feel unable to answer the questions," and they sit down. Your Honours, they haven't been deprived of the right to carry out an effective examination. They have simply chosen to accept the witness's answer, and that is not the same thing at all. My learned friends refer to answers given when they then move I think to deal with the probative value. To say that there was no probative value in the evidence of this witness relating to the Limaj trial because in answers to questions yesterday - and they cite to you a fairly -- a number of portions of transcript only from yesterday - he said that he couldn't now make a difference between 2005 and 2011. I'm particularly looking at 425, the transcript references at pages 10 -- at lines 10 to 15; and also 21 to 25. Your Honours will recall from the debate yesterday, this is an argument we had yesterday about this very matter, my submissions to you yesterday were - and remain the same - the witness is not saying what he said in 2005 was wrong; but merely that he can't now today remember how things were then. And then my learned friend I think referred to 425 -- sorry, 426, transcript lines 5 to 9, to suggest that it was beyond any doubt that the witness was not prepared to stand by his testimony. I don't have the precise quote and you'll forgive me if I paraphrase. But what that portion of the transcript says is this in answer to my question, perhaps I'll read the whole thing, lines 1 to 9: "When you answered the questions in 2005, did you do so in the best way that you could, trying to remember as well as you could what had happened, to give the Court as honest and truthful account as you could at that time, remembering what you could at that time?" He says: "That's where the problem lies, I can't recall that time, I can't tell between the time and the present time. I did my best, I hope -- I think to tell the truth because I don't -- I'm not used to lying. But now I'm really not in the state of mind to clarify things properly." And when one takes that with what he said previously in testimony 2 -- transcript 385 in answer to my question, very simple question, line 25: "Do you stand by what you said in the Limaj trial when you testified before the Court then? "A. Yes, on my evidence there, yes. "Q. What you said to that Trial Chamber was the truth, was it, Mr. Kabashi? "A. Yes. On my evidence before the court of law, yes, from what I recall." Your Honours, you also have to bear in mind the progression of the examination, and I think respectfully that is relevant. Questions of recollection arose during the course of that examination, and you will remember that this was not just about whether he remembered events but his whole demeanour and his whole manner would tend to suggest he had a variety of reasons as to why he was not prepared to testify. There are a legion, in fact, and remembering was only a small part of that, in our submission, and came right at the very end. And whether it is or is not true that he could or could not remember is a matter that has not been explored by the Defence. They had the opportunity to do that, should they so wish, but they did not. They simply accepted what he said. Because it's in their interests, certainly in the interests of Mr. Balaj and Mr. Harvey on one view - and it's not for me to tell them how to conduct their cases, but on one view - to test what Mr. Kabashi had to say about their clients in the Limaj case, as to whether what he said there was true or not. But they have chosen simply to accept that he feels unable to answer any questions. That is not a denial of the right and the exercise of a right to cross-examination or the exercise of a fair trial; it's simply a tactical decision that was made in the best interests of their clients at the time they made it. But objectively they have got and have had the opportunity to deal with this witness in any such way as they see fit, but they've chosen to simply accept what he said. He is there, he did answer some questions during the course of his examination-in-chief, not many I accept, but he did answer some. And as I've said, the demeanour of the witness would tend to suggest on one view that perhaps there were multiple reasons as to why he didn't want to testify. Your Honours, I can deal with some of those perhaps because this -- this application by the Defence is mounted on the supposition that that answer that he didn't remember is correct, should be accepted; and therefore, their right to a fair trial has been effectively denied because the man can't remember anything so they can't ask him any questions about it. I put it in the course of oral argument in a global way. My learned friends may object to the way I've put it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's simply not correct to suggest that we are asserting that the witness was necessarily telling the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let him finish. You will reply if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall, as the examination progressed, first of all the witness was trying to control questioning to some extent during the course of his examination, it began very early, transcript 334. It made Your Honours ask the question about his ethnicity. At the very beginning he had already begun to want to control what was happening. 342, line 11: "Get to the point. What do you want to know from me?" 343: "Don't beat about the bush." 356: "I won't allow you to ask questions. If you send me to prison, don't ask me any questions." He then had a whole series of statements during the course of his evidence where he demanded that there be no further questions of him, long before we get to memory issues. "I have no reason to answer your questions and you know why." T-355. 337: "May the gentleman on the right ask no further questions because I've got no answers to give." 339: "Why should I answer? What's the goal?" 344: "Q. Who was in charge of the group? "A. Will you tell me first why I was imprisoned here" -- Sorry. "Will you first tell me why I was imprisoned." 358, lines 9 to 11: "I can state here there is no justice at all. Don't ask me to answer questions, this is rubbish. What you're dealing with is absolutely rubbish." Line 18: "There is no justice as I can see. Take me to prison and keep me there if you like." 393: "Why should I feel obligated to answer it?" After Your Honour told him to answer a question. He was evasive and unwilling. Showing him the maps, Your Honour will recall answers like he had a poor schooling and wasn't good at reading maps, the clearest possible indication of the town, he couldn't even identify that. He demanded to know why others weren't being prosecuted or investigated. "Your investigators are worse than Serbs," he said, T-355. Your Honours will remember pages of rant, if I can put it in the vernacular. "You've done more committed crimes with your deeds." That's 356. 359: "You're the ones who ought to know. You're the ones who ought to have investigated. You ought to have worked." 392: "There are many many other things that have been disregarded, have not been investigated to come to justice," at which point Your Honour intervened and told him to stop. It wasn't his remit to inquire of the Prosecution why they had done what they had done, ordered him to answer the question and at page 393 still does not answer the question. And then he got to Mr. Kuci at 381, he said: "I cannot answer this question. It's not that I don't wish but I can't." 392: "He's now too late to speak about these things in my view. He's meaningless to talk about these things now." He's offering all the time his opinions about why he thinks what he thinks about the process, whether he's prepared to continue to answer questions. He gives a speech at T-397 after I'd again tried to get him to speak about Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi, referring to persons disappeared. T-400, he said to testify "was beyond me to do it." 401: "There's nothing more I can add to this trial, it's beyond me, it's impossible, I apologise for that." T-401, lines 14 to 15, after I asked him is he prepared to answer my questions, he said: "If I could I would do willingly but I cannot, I really cannot. I don't see any reason why." T-401, asked whether Limaj was true he just said: "I'm unable to discuss this issue further nor to answer more than I have done so far." And then at T-402: "I already stated it's not that I am unable -- it's not that I'm unwilling to reply to your questions but I'm unable to answer any other question and I cannot provide any more assistance to this Chamber. It's inside me." T-402, he carries on: "If the trial is here to do justice, to discover crimes and Prosecutor's office has done nothing, then why do you involve me? I'm a very insignificant player. I won't make any difference. I'm unable to speak about these things." And, Your Honours, at T-405, line 12, this: "No, I'm not afraid. But I am unable to testify. It's not a matter of fear. It's something inside of me, a feeling I have inside of myself, something that keeps you alive or makes you go on living in the place you live. There are many things that prevent me. I'm trying. I'm doing my best, but I can't. I don't see any right somewhere prevailing somewhere to give me a reason why. That's why I am not testifying. I said what I wanted to say," he goes on, "I don't think I can say something else." Your Honours, it appears that this witness has within him -- inside himself on one view what appears to be a moral compass that is not permitting him, for whatever reason, to speak. That may be one view. There may be other reasons, but it is not as simple as my learned friend's suggesting he just can't remember. There are multiple reasons. My learned friends have tactically - and I understand why, we all make tactical decisions - chosen not to question the witness. They have and have had an effective right and they have chosen to use it the way that they have. To meekly accept was their choice, but it's not right to say that the only reason this witness is unable to speak is because he alleges that his memory is failing. Your Honours, for those reasons my learned friends' application should be dismissed. First of all, the material that his -- that he provides within the Limaj transcript deals directly with the issues that Your Honour is facing -- Your Honours are facing, as Your Honours have already recognised in the, quite correctly, if I may respectfully say, in the decision that you have issued. The basis for exclusion would be the rights -- balancing that probative value against the rights to a fair trial. And, Your Honours, we say that fair trial has been safe-guarded, is safe-guarded, and continues to be safe-guarded. The fact that the defendants act the way they do through their counsel is entirely a matter for them. Your Honours, so far as the reference to the Witness 55 decision is concerned is simply not relevant in our submission, it's on a completely different point. It's a witness that started and didn't come back for cross-examination. This is not this case. The witness was there, in this courtroom, facing Your Honours, ready and able to be questioned; but my learned friends chose to act the way that they did. Your Honours, unless I can help you further, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Rogers. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all Your Honours have sat through these proceedings in relation to this witness and Your Honours will be aware of the background, of the history in front of Judge Orie, of what was described as the endless continuing story of this witness, his refusal to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, I'm personally not aware of what took place before Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's in the Appeals Chamber judgement that ordered this re-trial. This was a witness who was brought before the Court on several occasions and took the same sort of positions that he was taking here. In other words, he was not going to answer any substantive questions for a variety of different given reasons, other than fear. And it's certainly not the case that the Defence application under Rule 89(D) is premised on the proposition that this witness is telling the truth when he says that he can't remember. That may be part of his reason, there may be other reasons. Mr. Rogers would have it that he accepted that he had a moral compass which doesn't permit him to testify. Be that as it may, we all saw what happens to Mr. Rogers's attempts to get him to testify. He was not going to answer questions. Although he answered one or two at the beginning, as Mr. Rogers says you need to look at the progress of his examination, but the time we were more than half an hour in, every attempt by Mr. Rogers to ask him to engage at all with the facts was met with an answer which concluded with the statement: I am not prepared to answer your questions. I haven't counted the number of times the witness said: I am not prepared to answer, but we all know that they are legion. It is fanciful to suggest that were the Defence to attempt to cross-examine in the face of that and in the face of the clear statement of the witness that he was maintaining that position this morning when Defence counsel rose to cross-examine him, that we would have had anything more than the useless fanciful charade that went on when Mr. Rogers continued to press in the face of the witness refusing to answer. The suggestion that we meekly accept his assertion that he does not wish to testify is an absurd one. This is a witness who has committed and has been for years not to testify as to the substance. And it would be a fanciful distortion of what took place in this courtroom over the last few days to suggest that what the Defence did was anything other than what any responsible practitioner in this situation would do, which is to establish that the position he'd taken with Mr. Rogers as Prosecutor was the same position that he was going to take this morning when being cross-examined; and if it was, his position is: I am not going to testify. That is the situation that the court is faced with and anything other than a full recognition of that and an honest recognition of it would be a transparent distortion of what took place. These are not tactics. There comes a point when you draw a line. There is no point in me doing what Mr. Rogers had done, and then Mr. Harvey has do it and Mr. Guy-Smith, over and over and over again. Will you testify? No I won't. Will you testify? No I won't. It's pointless. That's the first thing. Secondly, what Mr. Rogers seems to be saying to you is that the witness was lying about his reasons in part. Yesterday he said to you in unequivocal terms that it was clear that the witness was having trouble with his recollection. That was the basis of the application that Mr. Rogers made yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: My learned friend knows that I said considerably more immediately after that and he should read into the transcript the whole of what I said which follows on directly from it so that it's clear that that isn't exactly what I said. That's part and I made it very clear what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He went on to say there may well be other reasons, but his primary position and the reason he asked Your Honours for the admission of the transcript was because it was clear, he said, that the witness was having difficulty recollecting. Well, it can't be clear and false at the same time. So the position is, says Mr. Rogers: Now I would like Your Honours to conclude that when he said that he was having difficulties recollecting, he's a liar. We take no position on that. Mr. Rogers can jump from one position to the other with a great fleetness of foot, but we take no position on it. You don't have to make a finding on that one way or another. But what we do respectfully submit is that Your Honours do need to grapple in the reasons and the ruling that you give with the answers that this witness gave yesterday in transcripts 424 to 426. And if Your Honours take the view that he was -- in doing those passages giving an account that he could not stand over his Limaj testimony -- because that's exactly what he says. He says: "I'm not in a position to give you an accurate answer as to whether what he said was right. I don't want to make mistakes because they will get me into more trouble. That's the problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You keep referring to that point. Is it your position that the statements that the witness made yesterday and through -- during these proceedings about what he thinks of his testimony in the Limaj trial are supposed to be determinative of the probative value of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, but Your Honours have cited an answer that he gave in your ruling -- a series of answers that he gave the day before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: With respect, if I may answer your question, in which Mr. Rogers put it to him was what you said true and he said yes. That is with the greatest respect an incomplete statement of the witness's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I accept that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm glad Your Honour does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will also remember that in the decision, the decision says he accepted that it was true in that trial and also said so in this trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, but with respect, he doesn't say that in this trial. On a fair reading of his evidence as a whole - and the passages that Your Honours did not refer to in the ruling - he significantly undermines that by saying he cannot say whether what he said in the Limaj case is true or reliable. He says it in terms. It's in black and white on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But here's my question to you: Are you saying what he says today affects the probative value of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- or is it what he said then?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, what affects the probative value of the testimony is that Your Honours have relied on a statement from him in these proceedings that the testimony in Limaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it's coupled with a statement he made to the Limaj trial when he made the declaration and he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that but he is now saying I do not know which parts of that testimony, if any, can be relied on. That's what he says in the transcript in page 424 to 426. Now, you may take the view he's lying when he says that. You may take the view he has other reasons and he's lying. In which case say so in your ruling, because that also is a conclusion that goes to the probative weight to be attached to his evidence if he's lied before you on oath. With the greatest of respect what Your Honours cannot do is to avoid addressing the answers that the witness gave which fundamentally undermine reliance on that transcript. You can't avoid addressing the question because it goes to his credibility. Either way. Either he was telling you the truth yesterday when he said: I can't remember whether what I told the Limaj court was true or false; or he's lying to you. But either way you can't avoid making a finding on that when you're concluding what probative weight you should attach to the Limaj transcript. It goes directly to it. So with the greatest respect there's an issue Your Honours need to grapple with and determine in the course of dealing with the 89(D) application. And I mean, were this matter to be considered further, it would obviously be of great assistance for the Appeals Chamber to know how Your Honours viewed those words and those qualifications, otherwise we would be speculating on what weight you'd attached to them and how you'd come to the conclusion that you had. So we would, with the greatest of respect, ask Your Honours to address that part of the transcript because it is so obviously germane to an evaluation of the witness's previous testimony's probative value that no proper assessment can be made under 89(D) without you having done it. Now, I recognise that it is possible for Your Honours to have made the decision in principle under 89(C) without reading the Limaj transcript because all that needs to be satisfied under 89(C) is that the evidence is relevant and probative, and you have been told by Mr. Rogers that it has reference to the Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi issue and on that basis you decided it was relevant and probative. But 89(D) requires you to conduct a relative evaluation on how probative it is and you can't possibly do that without having got to grips with the detail of the transcript and knowing what it is he actually said. And once you have done that, you will see it's a tiny proportion of that evidence that concerns this trial at all and that proportion of it was never the subject of testing or cross-examination. So, with respect, Your Honours now need, because 89(C) and 89(D) are different exercises; 89(D) requires you to actually decide how probative this material is and whether its probative weight is outweighed by the unfairness to the accused, that's something which, in order to do it properly, it's going to be necessary to consider which passages the Prosecution truly rely upon, for what they rely upon them, whether they are corroborated by other evidence in the case, what unfairness there is to the accused, and how to approach the testimony that the witness gave about his real reasons. And in particular, the testimony that he gave yesterday. And we would, as I say, invite Your Honours not simply to ignore those answers but to address them. Either you accept them or you reject them. If you accept them, they undermine the probative weight; and you reject them, then he was lying on oath, and that undermines the probative weight of it as well. We are in very dangerous territory here, in my respectful submission, and the only part of that transcript which is capable of corroboration is the passage originally relied upon by the Prosecution in the first trial, which is pages 4255 to 4260, which are the passages that deal with Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi. We would respectfully submit that even they fail the test of appropriate balance under Rule 89(D) but certainly anything going beyond that must do. Can I finally say this, Mr. Rogers didn't even address the question of probative value other than to just assert the Limaj transcript is probative. In the original trial the Prosecution was required to and did give a list of the page references that touched upon the issues in this trial, for obvious reasons, because that case was nothing to do with Jabllanice. It was a totally different area of Kosovo. And so it concerns a large amount of irrelevant material. It must be the case that those pages fall to be excluded under Rule 89(D) because they have no probative weight in these proceedings. They were never even relied on by the Prosecution in the first trial. And of the passages that were relied on, the only one with any corroboration, any independent evidence, is that the -- the passage that I've cited. And, Your Honours, we do respectfully submit in those circumstances that the balance is very, very squarely tipped in favour of exclusion, a decision that Your Honours can't properly evaluate without looking at the material, find out which passages Mr. Rogers says crossed the high probative threshold, where he says there's corroboration, and consider balancing that against this witness's actual testimony yesterday about what he was prepared to stand over in the Limaj trial. And the bottom line is he wasn't prepared to say which parts of it he could stand over and which parts of it he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Once again for purposes of brevity, I join in Mr. Emmerson's remarks. Given the history of this litigation and specifically referring to the Appeals Chamber decision in which this issue came up again, the suggestion that we bang upon a witness, a witness who has also indicated - and whether or not it's true or not, I don't know - but has indicated that he feels a victim with some sensitivity we have shown to people who do come into these courtrooms and discuss being victims, the notion that we bang upon a witness in order to get no answers, as we saw occur here for a day, not only I think is -- would be irresponsible from the standpoint of defending my client, but that is also ludicrous in terms of any argument that we would be able to obtain anything other than the answers that he gave. I am a bit concerned about one focus of Mr. Rogers's remarks, which he seems to be moving the argument into a question of what Mr. Kabashi remembered and that our application is based on a failure of memory. It is not a question of memory. That is one of the aspects of what occurred here. This gentleman made himself absolutely clear, and that clarity was as follows. And I am taking one part of an answer that he gave. "I did my best I hope ..." That's speculative --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can we have the reference, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's page 426, this is the passage that we've been through again and again and again, this is lines 1 through 9, starting at line 6 -- well, I'll start at line 5, I'll give -- read the whole answer. "That's where the problem lies. I can't recall that time. I can't tell between that time and the present time ..." That could be a function of memory, that could be a function of cognitive dissonance. We have no way of knowing. "I did my best ..." As to what? "I hope ..." Very well. As to what? He hopes he did his best as to what? " ... I think to tell the truth because I don't ..." "I did my best, I hope -- I think" -- his words, not my words. The difference of course being that I'm placing a different emphasis on them for the moment, but therein lies the rub because you don't have a clear answer to what's going on with this witness. "I'm not used to lying ..." Well, who is? Whenever in this courtroom have any of you heard anybody saying: I'm used to lying? You haven't. And most probably in your experience as Judges, the idea that somebody walks in and says: Well, I'm used to lying, that's what I do as a matter of course, that's the behaviour that I engage in, it's something that you haven't heard. If you have, then I find that that would be an extremely unique situation, and perhaps you have. "But now I really am not in that state of mind as to clarify things properly ..." That has nothing to do with memory. That has nothing to do with anything other than whatever his internal mechanisms are - which we won't know, although there have been some allusions to some medical difficulties, whether they be the case or not, I don't know. And what we are left with is a witness who refuses to testify. But his -- but his refusal - the manner in which it comes - is that he indicates: I can't answer your questions. So what are we supposed to do in that situation? The suggestion that Mr. -- that Mr. Rogers makes, that we -- that we weakly acceded to his assertions is not only insulting, it's also absurd. We all have sat in this room, we all watched him, we all watched his demeanour, we all saw how he answered, what he answered, when he answered. We haven't had the opportunity to cross-examine this man. You're left with not even a one-sided story. Submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I adopt everything said by Mr. Emmerson, everything said by Mr. Guy-Smith, but I'd just like to add this: In my submission it lies ill in the mouth of a Prosecutor to say: You had your chance to cross-examine, when he himself took the tactical decision not to ask Your Honours for permission that he could cross-examine the witness. If his position is that this witness was adverse to the Prosecution, he had a basis on which to ask Your Honours to allow him to treat this as a hostile witness and to cross-examine him. Instead of that, he took a tactical decision to slip in through the backdoor the evidence that he hoped that Your Honours would agree to him slipping in, which is evidence from a trial in 2005 in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just, Mr. Harvey, if I may interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is that a fair characterisation of the position taken by Mr. Rogers in this matter because the -- whereas I understand what you saying he took a tactical decision to do what he did, but isn't there a clear distinction between the procedure that would have been invoked had we gone -- had we had to go down the road of considering whether this was a hostile witness and the application that Mr. Rogers in fact made that the testimony in question was admissible under Rule 89(C) without more?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there is a distinction to be made between those two positions. The point that I am seeking to raise is - and I'm sure one that Your Honours will all accept - that written evidence from a previous case upon which a witness has not been cross-examined in this case and cannot be - and the Defence has been deprived of the opportunity of cross-examining him on that evidence - that evidence is by definition of far less probative value, of far less weight than evidence that has been cross-examined before Your Honours, where you have seen an opportunity for the questions to be asked and the answers to the given. That's why I say that this is evidence of a different character, a different quality, and not the kind of evidence which Your Honours would prefer, I'm sure, to have. I am sure you would prefer to have from the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not so that the decision admitting this evidence did, in fact, deal with the question of weight to be attached depending on the difficulties that you are raising?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have addressed or you have told us, of course, that you will determine what weight to attach to it. The problem that counsel always has in the Tribunal in this circumstance is we don't know how much weight you will attach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know in other jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say this is the trouble in the Tribunal. In other jurisdictions do you ever know what weight a Judge attaches to any evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The issue is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because I would like to be able to give you that determination if I -- if it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I am saying is that you will, of necessity, attach less weight to evidence that has not been cross-examined on, less weight to evidence that is only on paper, less weight to evidence that was given six years ago than you would do to a witness who is actually questioned before Your Honours, where you had had an opportunity to observe his demeanour in answering specific questions. I think that's a fundamental approach that any Tribunal would take. I'm not seeking to take it further than that, nor am I seeking to impugn your ruling this morning or your intention to evaluate these matters with the greatest of care. All I'm saying is that the Prosecutor - and again I understand his reasons, I hope - took a tactical decision not to seek to cross-examine this witness. And then he accuses the Defence of taking a tactical decision not to seek to cross-examine this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
